reasoning.Student A:
Because of the KEY PROPERTY, the set of schools I could possibly receive (my Obtainable Schools) is fixed given others' rankings and school priorities. My submitted ranking cannot change which schools are in that set — it only decides which school I get within that fixed set (I will receive my highest-ranked school among the obtainable ones).

Given that, the only way my ranking affects the outcome is to choose, among the schools that might be assigned to me, the one I most prefer. Therefore I should list schools in my true preference order so that, if a school is obtainable, I get the best one for me among that set.

Note also: many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, and my priorities are w:1, x:2, y:1, z:2. That may affect which schools are actually obtainable for me, but it does not change the conclusion: I should rank by my true preferences so I end up with the most preferred school that is in my Obtainable Schools.
reasoning.Student B:
The mechanism guarantees a fixed set of Obtainable Schools that my ranking cannot change; my submitted ranking only chooses which school I receive among that set (I get the highest-ranked school in the Obtainable Schools). Given that, the optimal strategy is to rank schools in true preference order so I obtain the best possible school from that fixed set.

My true preferences are z > y > w > x. My priorities are strongest (1) at x and z and weaker (2) at w and y. Other applicants predominantly prefer y > x > w > z, so competition for y and x is higher; that makes y less likely to be in my Obtainable set even though I prefer it over w and x. Regardless, since I cannot change which schools are obtainable, I should simply rank honestly so I get the most-preferred school among the Obtainable Schools.

Therefore I submit my true ranking: z > y > w > x.
reasoning.Student C:
Because the mechanism guarantees that the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my "Obtainable Schools") is fixed given others' rankings and schools' priorities, my own ranking cannot add any school to or remove any school from that set. My ranking only selects which school I get among those obtainable ones—the mechanism gives me the highest-ranked school in my submitted list that lies in my obtainable set.

Given that, there is no benefit to misrepresenting my true preferences to try to change which schools I might obtain (I cannot change that set). The only thing my ranking can do is decide which obtainable school I end up at. Therefore I should list the schools in my true preference order so that, whatever schools are in my obtainable set, I receive the best possible one according to my true tastes.

My true preference ordering is z > y > w > x. (I note that my priorities are relatively higher at w and x (rank 3) than at y and z (rank 4), and many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so in practice y might be less obtainable for me than w or x. But regardless of that, ranking strategically cannot change the obtainable set, so truthful ranking maximizes my chance of getting the best available school for me.)
